issues.explanation: Escape route planning implies a prominent ongoing external-danger/triggered-threat pattern in public places, but the formulation specifies no active links involving Triggers or Threat, and the rest of the profile is centered on bodily vulnerability and negative beliefs rather than situational danger. This makes the item poorly aligned with the formulation and cross-node content.

issues.item: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: Distrust of others is not impossible after a life-threatening accident, but in this profile it introduces an interpersonal/paranoid theme that is not supported by the other selected items or the formulation. The remaining items focus on bodily unreliability and permanent damage after an accident, so this item is the least coherent with the trauma-linked appraisal pattern presented.

vignette:
Khalid's Fracture

Khalid Mansour was seventy-five when a sheet of bronze fell on him in his studio. He had been working since dawn, as he had for fifty-three years, positioning a five-foot panel that was meant to be the centerpiece of a commission—an abstract meditation on loss, though he had not known then how intimately he would come to understand his own subject. The panel had been propped against a wooden frame, and the frame had given way without warning. There was a moment of terrible silence, then the weight came down across his lower back and left hip. He remembered the cold shock of the metal, the way his vision narrowed, the sound of his own voice—a sound he barely recognized—crying out in the empty studio. He lay there for nearly four hours before his daughter found him during her afternoon visit.

The hospital stay lasted two weeks. The doctors said he had been fortunate: two cracked ribs, a fractured pelvis, significant soft-tissue damage, but nothing that would not heal. They gave him a timeline, a regimen of physical therapy, prescriptions for pain. He came home to his small house in Pasadena with a walker and a daughter who rearranged his life to accommodate his fragility. What the doctors did not tell him—what no one could have told him—was that the fracture would not be the injury that would not heal.

Within weeks, Khalid had begun to believe that his body had betrayed him in some fundamental way. He could no longer trust it to hold him upright, to warn him of danger, to do what he asked of it. The ribs still ached when he breathed too deeply; the hip sent sharp reminders whenever he shifted his weight. But more than the pain itself, it was the unpredictability that terrified him. Because he was certain now that his body could fail him without warning, constant checking felt like the only rational response—pressing his fingers against his ribs to assess their stability, running his palm along his hip bone to confirm it was still there, lying awake at night monitoring the quality of his breathing. If his body was fundamentally damaged and could betray him at any moment, then staying out of the studio was not avoidance but necessary protection, the logical consequence of knowing himself to be broken. His body had become a stranger housing a threat he could not see coming. Because he was certain now that his body had been permanently damaged, that he had been fundamentally altered by what had happened, he found himself checking constantly—pressing his fingers against his ribs to assess their stability, running his palm along his hip bone to confirm it was still there, lying awake at night monitoring the quality of his breathing, cataloguing each twinge and flutter as evidence of some deeper, invisible injury that the doctors had missed. He had come to believe that his physical vulnerability was not a temporary condition but the new permanent state of his existence, and this conviction drove him to scrutinize himself relentlessly, as though constant vigilance might somehow prevent the next catastrophe. Because he was certain his body was fundamentally damaged and could betray him without warning, staying out of the studio was not avoidance—it was the only rational response to a genuine threat. The constant body checking, the sleepless nights spent monitoring his breathing, the refusal to exert himself: these were not symptoms to be overcome but necessary protections, the logical consequence of knowing himself to be broken.

His studio became a place he could no longer enter. The thought of being in that space, of standing near the frames and the bronze, of putting his body under any physical stress at all, filled him with a dread so complete that he simply stopped going. His daughter brought his mail there and locked the door. Khalid told himself he was being sensible, protecting what remained. But the avoidance only deepened his certainty that something was fundamentally wrong with him. He began to wonder—obsessively, in the small hours—why this had happened to him, what he had done or failed to do, whether God had decided that his time of making was over. The questioning offered no answers, only a kind of exhausting spiritual vertigo that left him more convinced than ever that he was broken beyond repair.

Now, six months later, Khalid sits in his daughter's living room most days. He has not held a sculpting tool since the accident. He does not sleep well. He is afraid to be alone, afraid of what his body might do, afraid that if he stops monitoring it for even a moment, it will fail him again. His daughter finally insisted he speak to someone. He came to the appointment because she asked, but he is not certain anything can be done. He is not the man he was, and he does not believe he ever will be again.
